newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: In Nicaragua, battle now turns to parliament.
newsitem.headline: In Nicaragua, battle now turns to parliament.

text.p: While Nicaragua's election gave an easy win to right-winger Arnoldo Aleman as president, his Liberal Alliance party's victory was less clear in the National Assembly, where a power struggle looms.

Neither the Liberals nor their left-wing Sandinista rivals won an outright majority in the Oct. 20 vote, leaving a National Assembly polarised between two bitter rivals with a handful of smaller parties holding the balance of power, top legislators said on Wednesday.
The assembly, commonly known as the parliament, was granted new powers over the budget, presidential appointments and foreign treaties by constitutional reforms passed in 1995.

"It will be a National Assembly polarised between the two principal powers with a group of small parties playing a very important role," legislator Luis Sanchez Sancho of the National Opposition Union (UNO) told Reuters.

He predicted a divisive legislative session as the powerful Sandinista bloc headed by former President Daniel Ortega tries to block Aleman's right-wing agenda. Ortega lost to Aleman by 51 to 37.7 percent but he and two other candidates got enough votes to win seats in the parliament.
The former Sandinista president has also refused to concede defeat, charging fraud in the presidential vote.

"Nobody, not even the Liberals, will be able to control the assembly. At the start the small parties will dominate, but only at the start," said legislator Julio Marenco, second secretary of the current National Assembly.

The final count gave the Liberals 42 of the National Assembly's 93 seats, followed by the Sandinistas with 37 and nine smaller parties with the remaining 14. The Liberals need 48 votes to pass legislation and 56 to amend the constitution.

"There will be an auction of these smaller parties. They will go to the highest bidder," Marenco said. And if Aleman wishes to govern effectively he must win that auction as the 1995 constitutional reforms go into effect in January, giving the assembly unprecedented powers and ending Nicaragua's tradition of a strong, often authoritarian president.

"While the Sandinistas didn't win the elections, they didn't lose, either. They will have 37 legislators led by a coherent, solid nucleus of leaders," Sanchez said. In contrast, he said, the Liberal Alliance, a coalition of four parties, is in danger of splintering into squabbling factions that would reduce its effectiveness.
